title: EU farm reform sparks fears of unequal funding across Europe
content:
European farmers may receive uneven financial support during the next round of the EU agricultural policy. Regional leaders fear that changing the rules for funding may end up supporting wealthier countries while neglecting rural development.

Funding for EU farms would be tied to national and regional partnerships in the new policy. The European Commission believes that this would give member states the flexibility to support their rural areas with other EU policies.

But various concerns were brought up during a high level meeting in Brussels as EU officials, parliamentarians and regional leaders discussed the next version of the Common Agricultural Policy (2028-2034). Regional leaders have asked for more guarantees on funding as well as a greater role in decision making.

The reform suggests that national governments can have greater autonomy in organizing farm support. But regional authorities are concerned that they could lose control over decisions that influence local farmers.

“The region cannot be simply somebody who is giving its advice.”
— MEP Herbert Dorfmann (EPP/ITA)

title: Prevention lacks one thing to win over finance ministers. Hard numbers
content:
The average European worker misses almost three weeks of work a year through sickness. A new study puts the cost to the EU at up to €810bn annually, roughly four per cent of its GDP. Yet governments still pour most of their health budgets into treatment rather than prevention.

Europe is losing workers and economic potential to illnesses that could be prevented. Its ageing population adds to the strain on social security systems and public finances. That is why health experts and policymakers argue that governments need to look seriously at prevention, not just at ways to treat disease.

At a conference in the European Parliament, health experts and policymakers warned that governments do not collect all the data they need. Without it, they cannot calculate the full cost of preventable illness, including lost working days, early retirement, and reduced productivity. The real question is whether Europe can afford to keep treating prevention as a secondary issue.

title: Sea to sky: How the new Frontex fragments migrant surveillance
content:
Frontex, the EU agency for the control of European borders, has allocated over €1bn for aerial surveillance in 2018–2028. The funding is growing rapidly: from €12m in 2018 to over €330m for next year.

Aerial surveillance is crucial for interceptions. According to LIMINAL, at least 33,000 migrants faced return to Libya and Tunisia between 2018 and 2024. The returns, by the security forces of those two countries, enjoyed the support of Frontex. (LIMINAL is a laboratory of the University of Bologna that investigates intersectional mobility and border violence.)

Lorenzo Pezzani, the mastermind of LIMINAL, told EU Perspectives that Frontex’s reform “comes as absolutely no surprise”. However, one of the main concerns is how Frontex “is playing a significant role in pushing for or enabling the use of drones within European civilian space”. The hotspot is the Central Mediterranean sea.

title: Can lighter green rules get Europe’s space sector off the ground?
content:
Last year, the US attempted 181 orbital launches, China 92, and Europe just eight. Lawmakers now want to narrow that gap with the bloc’s first common space rules. These would cover satellite safety, cybersecurity, and the environment, with less paperwork for smaller players.

Europe’s space sector moved a step closer to a single rulebook on Thursday. The European Parliament’s Industry, Research and Energy Committee approved its position with 73 votes in favour, one against, and two abstentions. The legislation, which the European Commission proposed in June 2025, would establish the first common EU rules for companies launching satellites, operating spacecraft, or providing space services in Europe. Currently, 13 EU countries have their own space legislation.

title: Journalism could get its first EU budget. If AgoraEU survives the cuts
content:
Artists, independent newsrooms, and civil society groups are caught in a tug of war over EU money. Lawmakers want to boost the bloc’s culture and democracy programme by a quarter. A Council proposal would cut it by almost a third.

The money would go to culture, independent journalism, and civil society. On Thursday, two Parliament committees adopted their position on the 2028–2034 AgoraEU programme, calling for €10.72bn. They were the Culture and Education committee and the Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs committee.

It passed with 64 votes in favour, 17 against, and two abstentions. More than 1,500 amendments were tabled to the Commission’s proposal, with MEPs Emma Rafowicz (S&D/FRA) and Alice Kuhnke (Greens/SWE) serving as co-rapporteurs.

Before the vote, Ms Rafowicz welcomed the compromise reached after difficult negotiations, but warned that Parliament’s ambitions would depend on securing sufficient funding during talks with EU governments. “Everything that we’re defending will never come to light if the budget doesn’t meet the expectations of the programme,” she told MEPs.

title: Parliament rejects ETS compromise, postpones crucial committee vote
content:
European Parliament’s industry and research committee postponed its vote on an opinion on emissions trading reform on Thursday after rejecting a compromise text. Rapporteur MEP Jüri Ratas (EPP/EST) requested the delay rather than proceeding through amendments individually.

Before the vote, Mr Ratas had urged colleagues to support the compromise, arguing that it offered industry more realistic conditions than the Commission’s proposal. “If we fail today, we risk losing some of our industries and jobs,” he said.

The Estonian lawmaker warned that companies could close or move production outside Europe to countries with less demanding rules. He described the text as an attempt to reconcile competing positions after intense negotiations.

The committee first rejected a motion to reject the proposal. It then voted on the compromise amendment by a show of hands, followed by a roll-call check. The compromise was rejected.

“Given that compromise has been rejected, I believe that it’s better to adjourn the vote than to vote through all the amendments individually,” Mr Ratas said.
snippet: European Parliament’s industry and research committee postponed its vote on an opinion on emissions trading reform on Thursday after rejecting a compromise text. Rapporteur MEP Jüri Ratas (EPP/EST)

title: Who runs the ECB? Capitals haggle as experts call for merit
content:
Borrowing costs for 350m Europeans may hinge on a deal between Berlin and Paris. Germany backs a Spaniard to lead the European Central Bank and claims the chief economist post for itself. France wants a seat too. Critics warn that national bargaining is crowding out merit.

After European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde announced her resignation in late October, European capitals quickly began manoeuvring to secure influence over the selection of her successor. With three of the ECB’s six Executive Board members due to leave in 2027, the negotiations extend beyond Ms Lagarde’s succession to a broader reshuffle of the bank’s top leadership.

Now, three weeks later, a deal is emerging. It would see a Spaniard lead the institution with German support, while Berlin takes the influential chief economist post. France, meanwhile, looks set to keep a seat on the bank’s Executive Board. The negotiations highlight how national interests can shape the leadership of one of Europe’s most powerful financial institutions.

title: Brussels pushes for AI classrooms while seeking limits for kids online
content:
The European Commission wants schools to help students navigate artificial intelligence. Education specialists warn that digital transformation requires trained teachers, funding and infrastructure.

European schools struggle with declining basic skills, teacher shortages and technological change. Brussels proposes the Education and Skills Package to improve digital literacy, support teachers, and help schools adapt to artificial intelligence.

The European Federation of Education Employers (EFEE) warns that “Schools across Europe face very different realities regarding infrastructure, funding and digital readiness, while many already struggle with teacher shortages and increasing workloads,” Daniel Wisniewski, secretary-general of EFEE, told EU Perspectives. “European ambitions must be matched by adequate resources and realistic implementation strategies,” he added.

For the schools, “main challenges include limited financial and human resources, unequal access to technology and the need to adapt working practices.” Mr Wisniewski said. The organisation also questioned why the previously announced roadmap for digital education to 2040 was not presented as a separate initiative.

creator: Joana Soares

title: Europe launches €95m semi-autonomous ship in Estonia
content:
The Union’s newest naval vessel is to provide surveillance and to protect undersea infrastructure. The EUROGUARD is not yet in service; developers say testing is the point of the exercise.

Europe has launched a new kind of naval vessel. The EUROGUARD semi-autonomous ship went through its launch in Nasva, Estonia, on the Baltic Sea. The 45-metre craft is to strengthen maritime surveillance and help protect Europe’s coasts. The European Commission says it will support member states facing growing risks at sea.

Those risks are real, according to the Commission. Threats to undersea cables, energy infrastructure, and strategic maritime routes are rising. The purpose of the vessel is to help member states respond to them.

The EUROGUARD project began in 2022. It brings together 29 organisations from 10 European countries. The Estonian shipyard Baltic Workboats coordinates the work. The European Defence Fund has contributed €65m of a total budget of about €95m.
snippet: The Union’s newest naval vessel is to provide surveillance and to protect undersea infrastructure. The EUROGUARD is not yet in service; developers say testing is the point of the exercise.

title: Outspend and outproduce Russia, Kubilius exhorts business summit
content:
Europeans are still too slow in paying the price of peace. The price of war would be higher, Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said on Wednesday.

Russia will spend about as much on its military next year as all EU member states combined, according to EU Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius. He made the claim at the European Business Summit in Brussels on 18 November 2026. For Mr Kubilius, the conclusion is stark. Europe is not yet deterring Moscow, and that must change.

The numbers are large. Russia plans to allocate €180bn to its military next year, a 33 per cent increase on this year. In purchasing power parity terms, that matches or slightly exceeds the €500–550bn that all member states will spend together. Mr Kubilius said Russia’s war economy remains able to expand production and to innovate.

Mr Kubilius said Russia was not being deterred. It was escalating attacks on Ukraine and waging a hybrid war against Europe. “We need first of all to outspend Russia in defence and to outproduce Russia in defence.” The question, he said, is whether the EU is doing enough at every level.
snippet: Europeans are still too slow in paying the price of peace. The price of war would be higher, Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said on Wednesday.
creator: Daniel Deyl

title: Mediterranean net is cast wide as Kallas’s absence raises eyebrows
content:
Security arrangements between the EU and its regional southern partners must address everybody’s concerns, the EU-MED Security Forum 2026 heard.

Hadja Lahbib opened the first EU–Mediterranean Peace and Security Forum in Brussels on Wednesday. It fell to the commissioner for equality as the planned keynote speaker, Kaja Kallas, head of the European External Action Service (EEAS) and EU security and foreign policy chief, was conspicuously missing.

The High Representative did not attend Wednesday’s scheduled appearance at the Schuman Security and Defence Forum, either. Her press office told EU Perspectives that Ms Kallas was down with flu. Whether it is a case of ‘political influenza’, an explanation that sprang to mind following major setbacks for Ms Kallas in recent weeks, was not clear at the time of writing.

Ms Lahbib opened the forum with a story from the 12th century. She described Al Idrisi, a cartographer commissioned by King Roger II of Sicily to survey the known world. The result, the Book of Roger, held detailed accounts of countries, cities, rivers, mountains, trade routes, and peoples.
snippet: Security arrangements between the EU and its regional southern partners must address everybody’s concerns, the EU-MED Security Forum 2026 heard.
creator: Daniel Deyl

title: EU strikes overnight deal for faster solar, grid, and charging permits
content:
Homes and businesses installing solar panels, batteries, or charging points could get permits within months. The smallest might need none at all. An EU deal also eases grid applications and makes larger renewable projects share benefits with locals.

Under the deal EU governments and Parliament reached early on Wednesday, permits for solar equipment and batteries installed alongside it would take no more than three months. Stand-alone storage and charging stations would have a six-month deadline. The agreed rules also set a three-month limit for grid connections, extendable to six months where justified.

“We need grid infrastructure for clean, affordable, and homegrown energy and to break our dependence on imported fossil fuels,” said Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment, whose country holds the rotating Council presidency. He spoke after the provisional agreement. Electricity transmission projects currently take around ten years to complete, with permitting accounting for more than half that time.

title: Experts back EU advanced materials plan but warn of costly road to market
content:
Lighter aircraft, better batteries, and plastics made from plants. Europe is good at inventing new materials, less so at making them. Brussels’ new plan to change that wins praise. But it is not binding, and its success rests on national governments.

Advanced materials include things like lightweight composites used in aircraft and cars, new materials for batteries and magnets, and bio-based alternatives to conventional plastics. Engineered to have specific properties, they can make products lighter, stronger, more efficient, or more sustainable. On 18 November, the European Commission presented an agenda to turn Europe’s strength in research into industrial leadership in this field.

The Commission’s proposal for an Advanced Materials for Europe agenda sets three benchmarks for 2035: a 20 per cent increase in research and innovation investment, 20 per cent more EU-based start-ups and scale-ups, and more projects reaching higher levels of industrial deployment, all compared with 2023. It also calls on member states to coordinate research priorities and improve access to testing facilities, industrial scale-up, and skills.

title: Is Europe’s Rwanda deportation plan just a political bluff?
content:
Rejected asylum seekers in five EU countries could soon be flown to Rwanda. Rights groups and opposition lawmakers hope the plan never takes off, since British judges have already sunk a similar scheme.

For Rwanda, this is familiar territory. This week in Vienna, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands unveiled their plan to turn the country into the first return hub outside the EU. A pilot centre for about 100 people should open in 2027, although no deal has been signed yet.

Kigali has already entered into similar arrangements with the US. It also tried to strike such deals with Britain and Israel, but courts stepped in. The British Supreme Court cited the risk of violating the UN Refugee Convention, specifically the ban on refoulement.

Yet as early as 2021, Denmark launched a process to externalise asylum procedures to Rwanda. Its government, led by the Social Democrats, nonetheless takes a hardline stance on migration. The African Union responded sharply at the time: “Such attempts to stem out migration from Africa to Europe is xenophobic and completely unacceptable.” What has changed?
